newsitem.title: USA: Clinton, Mubarak meet as Mideast tensions flare.
newsitem.headline: Clinton, Mubarak meet as Mideast tensions flare.

text.p: President Bill Clinton met Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak on Monday as new tensions flared in the Middle East over Israeli plans to withdraw from the West Bank.

The meeting was one of a series between Clinton and the main regional players as Washington assesses how to proceed towards a comprehensive peace settlement despite a backdrop of continuing Israeli-Palestinian strife.

The top Palestinian negotiator resigned on Monday to protest Israel's decision to hand back nine percent of the territory it occupies in the West Bank, rather than the 30 percent the Palestinians had expected.

The decision appears to have worsened Israeli-Palestinian relations already strained by Israel's plan to build 6,500 housing units for Jews in Arab East Jerusalem and its moves to shut down four PLO offices in East Jerusalem.
Clinton and Mubarak made no comment on the withdrawal plan as they began a one-on-one Oval Office meeting, putting off questions until a news conference at 2:30 p.m. EST (1730 GMT).
The two were to be joined by their senior advisers and then hold a working lunch before the news conference.

Mubarak is the third Middle Eastern leader to meet Clinton at the White House in the past month, following Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's visit on February 13 and Palestinian President Yasser Arafat's visit on March 3.
Jordan's King Hussein is due here for talks next Tuesday.
Earlier on Monday, Arafat said Israel's decision on the West Bank pullout, the first phase of which was expected to go forward this week, had violated Netanyahu's peace promises.

"There is a real crisis because there is a clear breaching to what had been agreed upon," Arafat told reporters in Gaza, calling the Israeli decision "a trick and a conspiracy against the peace process."

Arafat spoke after top Palestinian negotiator Mahmoud Abbas, better known as Abu Mazen, submitted his resignation to protest Israel's decision to hand over nine percent of the West Bank instead of the 30 percent Palestinians expected.

Abbas, an architect of the groundbreaking 1993 Israel-PLO peace accord, demanded in talks with Israeli Foreign Minister David Levy on Sunday that Israel consult Palestinians on the scope of withdrawal.

The pullback from parts of the West Bank occupied by Israel since 1967 is the first of three outlined in a 1995 peace accord and reaffirmed in an agreement on a partial withdrawal from the West Bank town of Hebron that Netanyahu signed in January.
Neither agreement sets out the scope of the pullbacks, and Israel says a U.S. note attached to the Hebron deal left the extent of the withdrawal to its sole discretion.
At last week's meeting with Arafat, Clinton criticised Israel for its decision to build additional housing for Jews in Arab East Jerusalem, saying it bred mistrust in the region.
But the United States last week vetoed a U.N. Security Council resolution that would have called on Israel to abandon the plans for housing settlement.
Clinton said on Monday he did not think it fair to say he had "sanctioned" the settlement. He declined further comment.

Mubarak received a cooler welcome from the Anti-Defamation League, a Jewish group that fights racism. It took out a full-page advertisement in The New York Times asking him to "stop the anti-semitic hate in Egypt." The ad showed Egyptian cartoons of Israeli soldiers carrying flags with the Nazi swastika emblazoned on them.
